commenti.body:
Last year's Housekeeping for Beginners would fit this perfectly.

It's about a woman who finds herself in the position of having to raise her girlfriend's children, and the tenuous family that they create for themselves along with her gay male friend, his lover, and the various friends and queer youth that have been adopted into their lives.

Gregg Araki's Totally F***ed Up would be a great addition as well, which is essentially a queer gen x take on Masculin Feminin.

I mean, I feel like, when you boil them down to their purest essence, a huge percentage of movies starring LGBT characters are in a way or another either about (traditional) family life and how it's affected by a character's identity or orientation, or about their journey towards a new, chosen, family, so the pool of stuff you could pick from is pretty big.

If you wanna go for the most obvious, safest pick, maybe The Kids Are Alright, which is literally about a LGBT family, pretty self explanatory, and also it's a pretty nice movie. If you want something more out-of-the-way, edgier, with a loosest connection to the family theme and more about finding your own group of people, I just rewatched Hedwig and The Angry Inch and yeah, I'm pretty sure I could sell it as a movie about families if I had to.

*Tokyo Godfathers* (2003) really plays with the chosen family idea. The three main characters (or at least 2 of them) maintain a front of sticking together out of convenience when to us it's obvious that they love each other. One thing about family is you often can't help loving each other even when you can't stand each other.

The movie gives us a family with the traditional roles: a mother, father, and a teenage daughter decide to adopt an infant. But the characters have more or less fallen into these roles subconsciously rather then purposely constructed them. And so the movie interrogates: what even is a "mother," a "father," a "daughter," or a "family."

**The Birdcage** (*Mike Nichols, 1996*)   
A young man brings his fiancées deeply conservative parents home to meet his father … who unfortunately owns a drag bar with his long term boyfriend. Shenanigans ensue as they try to play it straight and make a good impression for the sake of their son. It’s actually a remake of a French farce from the 70’s called La Cage aux Folles, which is also very good if you’re feeling a bit classier.

**But I’m A Cheerleader** (*Jamie Babbit, 1999*)   
A comedy about conversion therapy! Found family in the widest possible sense, it’s about finding your people and how you belong, but it’s very funny and sweet.

**20,000 Species Of Bees** (*Estibaliz Urresola Solaguren, 2023*)   
A young trans girl spends a summer with the women of her family, as they all come to terms with their places in the world. I must confess I haven’t actually seen this one, but a friend has raved about it since she saw it by chance. She cried, in a good way.

**Iron Ladies** (*Youngyooth Thongkonthun, 2000*)   
Based on a true story about a real Thai volleyball team made up of gay men and trans women (sort of, it’s complicated). It’s found family in the way all sports movies essentially are, though with the added twist that their actual families are a major plot kink!

**Paris Is Burning** (*Jennie Livingstone, 1990*)   
A documentary about the NYC ball scene, with all its attendant drag queens, trans people and street kids, alongside their odd living arrangements: part sorority, part sports team, part family. A remarkable record of a way of life that doesn’t really exist anymore, though its legacy has been complicated by accusations of poor compensation for the subjects.

**Party Monster** (*Fenton Bailey/Randy Barbato, 2003*)   
A dramatisation of the Club Kids era of New York’s queer nightlife, essentially the uptown equivalent to the Ball Scene. Drugs! Sex! Murder! Quite a lot more drugs! Seriously, you won’t believe how many drugs they do! There’s a documentary also called Party Monster that covers the same basic era, though focuses much more heavily on the scandal rather than the culture.

ANY John Waters movie pretty much fits the bill. The theme of found-family amongst queer characters runs through his entire filmography. Cry Baby or Hairspray are probably the most family-friendly and accessible.

Thanks a lot! I will surely check them out.  
(I also thought about But I'm a Cheerleader and 20,000 Bees but we already showed those recently)
Tokyo Godfahters was already planned as the final movie of the month, so I am glad you found it fitting as well :)
Housekeeping sounds really interesting, unfortunately it doesn't seem to have a theatrical release in Germany.

That's a shame! It doesn't seem like it was widely seen in general, which is too bad considering it was beautifully shot and had a very humanist touch.

Hopefully it'll get picked up for streaming at some point and reach a wider audience!
